core: Absolute advantage: producing more of a good with the same inputs
Comparative advantage: producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer
Mutually beneficial trade is possible even when one party has an absolute advantage in every good
Worked two-country, two-good example computing opportunity costs and identifying comparative advantage
Gains from specialization: total output rises when each party specializes by comparative advantage
Terms of trade: a trading price between the two parties' opportunity costs makes both better off

The general concept of opportunity cost (owned by opportunity-cost topic)
Tariffs and other trade barriers (owned by tariffs topic)

claims.claim: A country (or party) has an absolute advantage in a good if it can produce more of that good with the same resources.
A party has a comparative advantage in a good if it can produce that good at a lower opportunity cost than another party.
The principle of comparative advantage was formulated by David Ricardo in his 1817 book On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation.
Even when one country has an absolute advantage in producing all goods, both countries can still benefit from trade by specializing according to comparative advantage.
When each party shifts production toward the good in which it has a comparative advantage, combined (total) output rises.

In the worked example (Northland 6 wheat or 3 cloth per worker-day; Southland 2 wheat or 2 cloth), Northland's opportunity cost of one cloth is 2 wheat and Southland's is 1 wheat, so Southland has the comparative advantage in cloth and Northland in wheat, even though Northland has the absolute advantage in both goods.

In the worked example, holding combined cloth output fixed at 150 units, reallocating labor toward each party's comparative-advantage good raises combined wheat output from 240 to 300 units (a gain of 60) with no loss of cloth.

Trade benefits both parties only when the terms of trade (the exchange ratio) fall between the two parties' opportunity costs; in the example, a price of cloth between 1 and 2 wheat per cloth makes both better off.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 33.1: Absolute and Comparative Advantage
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19 via WebFetch. Supports: absolute advantage as producing more of a good with the same resources; comparative advantage as producing a good at a lower opportunity cost ('lower cost in terms of other goods'); the method of deriving each country's opportunity cost from production numbers; and that the party with the lower opportunity cost has the comparative advantage. The section's own illustration (Saudi Arabia/United States, oil/corn, per-hour figures giving Saudi Arabia comparative advantage in oil and the US in corn) was used only to confirm the method; the lesson's worked example uses original Northland/Southland wheat/cloth numbers. No passages reproduced beyond short definitional phrases.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 33.2: What Happens When a Country Has an Absolute Advantage in All Goods
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19 via WebFetch. Supports: even when one country has an absolute advantage in all goods and another has an absolute disadvantage in all goods, both can still benefit from trade; that shifting production toward each party's comparative advantage raises combined output; and that mutually beneficial terms of trade lie between the two parties' opportunity costs (the section works a US/Mexico shoes-and-refrigerators example with explicit gain/loss offsets and trade-range bounds). Used to ground the 'absolute advantage in everything' result, the total-output-rises claim, and the terms-of-trade range. No passages reproduced beyond short definitional phrases.
